from 19 months to nine. We brought the institutions of the World Bank Group together

• Greater efficiency

and eliminated bureaucratic duplication, making it faster and easier for us to

The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by
initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water
Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected

The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly,

The World Bank Group is part of a pool of international lenders providing
financing for the project: In fiscal 2026, the Board approved an IFC loan of

AND JOBS
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of
finance to a platform that channels global capital
flows into developing countries. Rather than
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and
our convening role to crowd private capital into the
most productive sectors for job creation. This means
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool
of global capital to development opportunities.
In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that
are already translating into results. While financing
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years,
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

For the first time, the World Bank Enterprise Surveys
have achieved global coverage, delivering critical
indicators for 164 economies to pinpoint constraints
to private investment and job creation, effectively
complementing the Business Ready project by
directly capturing the voice of the entrepreneur.
Women, Business and the Law 2026 measured,
for the first time, perceptions of how consistently
laws supporting women’s economic participation
are enforced — finding that, on average, economic
opportunity laws are only half enforced. Global Findex
2025 provided the world’s only comprehensive study
of financial inclusion and how adults around the world
access and use financial services.

We have fully embraced AI tools at the World Bank
Group, and we support clients to adopt, adapt, and
then advance them for their own needs. Our client
engagements focus on Small AI — affordable, fitfor-purpose solutions designed for local conditions,
including places with limited power, connectivity,
and computing capacity. This is not a second-best
path. It is a practical way to strengthen workers,
help firms grow, improve services, support local
entrepreneurs, and create more and better jobs.
There is much more to do, and no institution
can meet the jobs challenge alone. But this
year demonstrated what is possible when our
shareholders, clients, partners, and staff work
together with urgency and purpose.
The World Bank Group is faster, simpler, and
better equipped to deliver. Now we must build
on that progress — and help create more jobs for
more people.

The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by
initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water
Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected
to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply.
The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly,
approximately 29,000 jobs, as well as advancing long-term job creation.
The World Bank Group is part of a pool of international lenders providing
financing for the project: In fiscal 2026, the Board approved an IFC loan of
up to $375 million. IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million
concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green
Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of
up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan
Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This
is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water
reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness.
The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our
Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments,
long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water

Brazil’s family farms employ nearly 10 million people and play a central
role in food production. Our partnership with the government, launched
in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved
technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030.
This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority
that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus.
Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique
capabilities. First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations
of family farms by investing in physical and human capital, such as rural
roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards,
repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. Finally,
the World Bank Group expands access to finance through MIGA’s
guarantees and insurance, as well as partnerships created by the
World Bank and IFC. The private sector is a critical partner across
all three pillars.

• IFC projects delivered health, nutrition, and
population services to 36.2 million people,
improved education for 2.8 million students, and
IFC’s engagements with private companies helped
nine countries strengthen their capacity to prevent,
detect, and respond to health emergencies.
• Through infrastructure investments, IFC helped
68.2 million people get improved access to
sustainable transport infrastructure and services
and 86.1 million people to gain electricity access,
enabled 19.5 gigawatts of renewable energy
capacity, and provided 6.2 million people with
water, sanitation, and/or hygiene. IFC projects in
the digital sector reached 193.5 million people
using broadband internet and 152.1 million people
using digitally enabled services.
• IFC projects with financial institutions enabled
125.5 million individuals and firms to gain access to
financial services, including 63.6 million women or
women-led enterprises.

The World Bank Group is also offering Ukraine comprehensive financial and technical
support. Re-PoWER, a World Bank trust fund-financed project, secured $403 million in
grants to restore electricity and heating for millions of people. In fiscal 2026, more than
$150 million of these grants were allocated for heating units, as well as for equipment
needed to secure power imports from the EU. Another project is rehabilitating
hydropower plants and delivering reliable power to affected communities.

Also in
fiscal 2026, Italy joined eight other IFC development
partners — Belgium, the European Commission, France,
Japan, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland, and
the United Kingdom — to support IFC’s investment
program in Ukraine, which helps sustain critical sectors
and supports Ukraine’s reconstruction, including
agribusiness, energy, and technology, and enables
businesses to continue operating despite security risks,
labor shortages, and rising input costs. IFC trust funds
have now received more than $1 billion in concessional
finance commitments for Ukraine.

CATALYZING PRIVATE SECTOR INVESTMENT
While the World Bank builds public sector foundations,
IFC catalyzes private sector investment, mobilizing
private capital with support from development
partners. In fiscal 2026, IFC deployed nearly
$1.4 billion in partner funding across its blended
finance, upstream, and advisory activities, helping
transform markets, mobilize investment, and support
job creation in challenging environments. This
sustained donor support reflects the strength of IFC’s
longstanding relationships with development partners.
IFC’s blended finance trust funds provide concessional
donor funding, combining it with IFC’s own-account
financing to make high-impact projects viable in
challenging markets. On average, from fiscal
2018–2026, every dollar of blended finance helped
unlock more than $6 in total investment.

food and nutrition security for 44.1 million people.
• Through IFC projects in various sectors,
13.8 million people benefited from actions to
advance gender equality, 46.9 million people

more than 250,000 people either displaced or in
host communities were provided with services and
livelihoods, over 400,000 hectares of terrestrial
and aquatic areas benefited from enhanced
conservation/management practices, and
$61.8 billion in private investments resulted
from IFC interventions.

Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a
quarter of GDP. But for years, the sector has been constrained by a narrow
model dominated by all-inclusive resorts in only two of the archipelago’s
10 islands, with few links to local businesses. Infrastructure deficits, a
shortage of skilled hospitality workers, and the absence of a coherent
framework for attracting quality investment left the country exposed and
its potential unrealized.
The World Bank Group has worked across its private and public sector
arms to help Cabo Verde chart a more diversified and inclusive tourism
sector. Two World Bank operations — the Resilient Tourism and Blue
Economy Development Project and the Improving Connectivity and Urban
Infrastructure Project — are strengthening the sector’s governance and
institutional framework, while upgrading critical infrastructure, including
coastal and jetty facilities, maritime passenger terminals, heritage sites,
and public spaces.

REINSURANCE
Since 1997, MIGA has successfully used reinsurance to
leverage its investment guarantee capacity, manage
its portfolio risk profile, and foster the growth of the
private political risk insurance market. Significant
benefits have accrued both to MIGA’s investors, who
have gained access to higher levels of coverage for
projects in developing countries, and to host countries,
which have benefited from much higher levels of
productive foreign investment.

under IFC’s Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises
(MSME) Finance Platform illustrates how close World
Bank Group collaboration can expand financing for
MSMEs, one of IFC’s key priorities. Supported by the
IDA Private Sector Window trust fund, this program
provides guarantees to private financial intermediaries.

financing, together mobilizing $224 million in

capital — an 11-fold multiple of the trust fund allocation,

private investment in MSME finance.

nearly $50 billion through Sustainable Development
Bonds issued in a variety of structures and maturities.

The Executive Directors are encouraged to see
new targets driving real change and maintaining
the World Bank Group’s focus on job creation.
The Target Map, launched in fiscal 2026, aligns
our ambitions against 10 strategic priorities that
enable job creation, including AgriConnect, Mission
300, and Water Forward. The institution continues
to make vital progress toward the ambitious goal
of delivering quality, affordable health services
to 1.5 billion people by 2030. Alongside these
health initiatives, the Board emphasizes the
importance of ongoing efforts to empower women
by expanding their access to social protection and
credit. The Board strongly supports the World

broadband connectivity, strengthen digital systems
and data infrastructure, and build the digital and
AI skills necessary for workers to participate in
an AI-enabled economy.

The World Bank Group Guarantee Platform,
hosted at MIGA, continues to play a vital role in
bringing private capital to emerging markets.
The Board commends MIGA for surpassing
$100 billion in cumulative guarantee issuance
since its founding in 1988, a remarkable
achievement from just $366 million in paid-in
capital. In addition, in fiscal 2026, the World Bank
Group surpassed its goal of $20 billion in annual
guarantee issuance — four years ahead of the
2030 target.

Bank Group’s Climate Change Action Plan, a

external partnerships to generate new ideas. In fiscal
2026, the World Bank Group and partners launched a
new Mission 300 Private Sector Council to mobilize
the billions in private investment needed to connect
300 million Africans to electricity by 2030, and unlock
job creation across the continent. The Council,
comprising 14 leaders from diverse sectors, will help
drive strategies to accelerate commercial investment
that supports both energy access and employment.

holding back private investment in emerging markets.

Advisory Council on Jobs in 2024 to develop actionable

government to provide new, outside-in thinking.

and eliminated bureaucratic duplication, making it faster and easier for us to

Established in 1999, the Office of the Compliance

The decision drew on more than a year of deliberation and was informed by the
recommendations of a Task Force engaged by the Boards. The Task Force carried
out consultations with internal and external stakeholders, including several webinars,
learning sessions with other multilateral development banks, and a written
comment period.

Convention and Additional Facility. The background
paper examines how contract-based dispute resolution

analytical guide and practical reference for investors,

MIGA completes the World Bank Group’s integrated
approach by using trust funds to provide guarantee

and Gaza Trust Fund, and the Support for Ukraine’s

To achieve this, we are working with all clients as One World Bank Group,
in close partnership with other multilateral institutions, the private sector,
and civil society. The World Bank Group includes:
• International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD),
which provides financial products and policy advice to help countries reduce
poverty and extend the benefits of sustainable growth to all their people.
• International Development Association (IDA),
which provides grants and concessional loans to low-income countries.
• International Finance Corporation (IFC),
which mobilizes private capital at scale, supports businesses from
microenterprises to large corporations, and creates jobs that drive economic
growth and opportunity.
• Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA),
which houses the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform, providing
guarantees to mobilize private capital for developing countries.

AND JOBS
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of
finance to a platform that channels global capital
flows into developing countries. Rather than
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and
our convening role to crowd private capital into the
most productive sectors for job creation. This means
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool
of global capital to development opportunities.
In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that
are already translating into results. While financing
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years,
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

THROUGH GUARANTEES
The government of Japan and MIGA deepened a
long-standing partnership to scale up the mobilization
of private capital in developing countries. Japan
committed nearly $20 million in additional funding to
MIGA-administered trust funds, reinforcing its position
as a leading contributor and strategic partner. This
support will expand MIGA’s ability to deploy political
risk insurance and trade finance guarantees in fragile
and conflict-affected situations — including Ukraine and
the West Bank and Gaza — as well as to advance energy
transition projects in emerging and frontier markets
with a focus on Sub-Saharan Africa. The partnership
underscores Japan’s continued leadership in leveraging
innovative financing solutions through the World
Bank Group Guarantee Platform to crowd in private
investment where it is most needed and where risks
remain highest.

On March 6, 2026, President Nasry Juan Asfura of Honduras signed the ICSID
Convention in Washington, D.C., making Honduras the 166th Signatory State to the

insurance companies can invest. The $510 million
transaction was listed on the London Stock Exchange,
giving visibility, pricing transparency, liquidity, and
the prospect of secondary trading. The second
transaction under the EMSP was completed in June

co-investment from the UK Government’s Mobilist
Program alongside IFC.
